then.text: Carmen rang. She says you're a treasure. I say she should write her lunch on her hand.
Go on, before it gets cold! And if that van man is still shouting, you have my permission to shout back.

else.text: Carmen forgot her lunch again? Of course she did. Here: tortilla, bread and an orange. She's thirty-eight and I still pack it.

When they shut the frontier in 1969 my mother lost her job on the Rock overnight. Thousands did. So when it opened again, I said: my children will cross it every day, and they'll have a good lunch doing it.
Mind the van driver at the back of the queue. He's been there since dawn and he's in a mood. You may have to settle it the usual way.
Buenas. Sit down, have a caña. That's a small beer, the small one, because it's hot and you're not on holiday. Or you are. Either way.
The tortillitas are from my grandmother's recipe. Chickpea flour, shrimp, a little onion and parsley. And a fryer older than me.

lal_waiter.text: If you want to order like a local: 'Una caña, por favor', a small beer, please. 'La cuenta, por favor', the bill, please. 'Gracias', thanks.
And 'buenas'. Round here we drop the rest of 'buenos días' and just say 'buenas'. It saves energy for the important things, like lunch.

lal_regular.text: Lunch here is at three. Dinner is at ten. Tea is at nobody-knows. You'll adjust.
In summer the whole town comes out after dark, when it's cool. Children on the plaza at midnight, grandmothers on chairs in the street. It's the best part of the day.
